The settlement of Sireniki is indicated with the red and yellow dot. | map2 = Lang Status 01-EX.svg | mapcaption2 = {{center|{{small|Old Sirenik is classified as Extinct by the [[UNESCO]] ''[[Atlas of the World's Languages in Danger]]''}}}} }} '''Sirenik''', '''Sirenik Yupik''',[http://www.language-archives.org/language/ysr OLAC resources in and about the Sirenik Yupik language] '''Sireniki Yupik'''[https://gcrc.carleton.ca/confluence/display/ISIUOP/Sireniki+Sea+Ice+Dictionary Sireniki Yupik Sea-Ice Dictionary] (also '''Old Sirenik''' or '''Vuteen'''), or '''Sirenikskiy''' is an extinct [[Eskaleut language]]. It was spoken in and around the village of [[Sireniki]] ({{lang|ru|Сиреники}}) in [[Chukotka Peninsula]], [[Chukotka Autonomous Okrug]], [[Russia]]. The [[language shift]] has been a long process, ending in total [[language death]]. In January 1997, the [[terminal speaker|last native speaker]] of the language, a woman named '''Vyjye''' (Valentina Wye) ({{langx|ru|Выйе}}), died.{{sfn|Vakhtin|1998|p=162}}{{cite book |language=ru |author=Николай Вахтин [Nikolai Vakhtin] |year=2000 |title=Язык сиреникских эскимосов: Тексты, грамматические и словарные материалы |trans-title=The Language of the Sirenik Eskimos: Texts, Grammatical and Dictionary materials |place=Munchen |publisher=Lincom-Europa |url=http://www.eu.spb.ru/univ/rector/index.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070910134859/http://www.eu.spb.ru/univ/rector/index.htm |archive-date=2007-09-10 |isbn=9783895869518}}{{cite web |language=ru |work=Поддержка прав коренных народов Сибири |trans-work=Support for Siberian Indigenous Peoples Rights |title=ЭСКИМОСЫ |trans-title=Eskimos |url=http://www.nsu.ru/ip/eskimos.php |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070830162420/http://www.nsu.ru/ip/eskimos.php |archive-date=2007-08-30}} Ever since that point, the language has been [[Extinct language|extinct]];{{sfn|Vakhtin|1998|p=162}} nowadays, all [[Sireniks]] speak [[Siberian Yupik language|Siberian Yupik]] or [[Russian language|Russian]]. Despite this, censuses as late as [[2010 Russian census|2010]] report up to 5 native speakers of Sirenik.{{Cite web |date= |title=tab6.xls |url=http://www.gks.ru/free_doc/new_site/population/demo/per-itog/tab6.xls |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180206181745/http://www.gks.ru/free_doc/new_site/population/demo/per-itog/tab6.xls |archive-date=2018-02-06 |access-date=2024-07-04 |website=gks.ru}} {{lang|ysr|Сиӷы́ных}} {{IPA|ysr|siˈʁənəx|}} is the endonym for the eponymous settlement of Sireniki.{{sfn|Menovshchikov|1964|p=7}}{{sfn|Menovshchikov|1964|p=195}} The endonym for the people itself is {{Lang|ysr|сиӷы́ныгмы̄́ӷий}} ({{IPA|ysr|siˈʁənəɣˈməːʁij|}}; {{gloss|Sirenikites}}); the singular form is {{Lang|ysr|сиӷы́ныгмы̄́ӷа}} {{IPA|ysr|siˈʁənəɣˈməːʁa|}}.{{sfn|Menovshchikov|1964|p=195}}{{sfn|Menovshchikov|1964|p=31}} This article is based on Menovschikov (1964),{{sfn|Menovshchikov|1964}} with cited examples transliterated from Cyrillic transcription to the [[International Phonetic Alphabet]]. == Classification == === Genealogical === ==== External ==== Sirenik is an Eskimoan language, one of the two major groupings of the [[Eskaleut languages]]. The exact [[Language family|genealogical classification]] of Sirenik within its group is uncertain. Some argue that Sirenik is a remnant of a third group of Eskimoan languages, in addition to [[Yupik languages|Yupik]] and [[Inuit languages|Inuit]] groups{{sfn|Vakhtin|1998|p=161}}{{cite web |script-title=ru:Языки эскимосов |work=ICC Chukotka |publisher=[[Inuit Circumpolar Council]] |language=ru |url=http://www.icc.hotbox.ru/yaziki.htm}}[http://www.philology.ru/linguistics4/menovshikov-97a.htm Menovshchikov 1997] (see a visual representation by tree and an argumentation based on [[comparative linguistics]]{{cite web |url=http://www.uaf.edu/anlc/groups/ |author=Gary Holton |title=Alaska Native Language Relationships and Family Trees |publisher=University of Alaska Fairbanks |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110429051331/http://www.uaf.edu/anlc/groups/ |archive-date=2011-04-29}}{{cite web |url=http://www.uaf.edu/anlc/resources/yupik-inuit/ |author=Lawrence Kaplan |title=Comparative Yupik and Inuit |publisher=University of Alaska Fairbanks |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110805204303/http://www.uaf.edu/anlc/resources/yupik-inuit/ |archive-date=2011-08-05}}); others regard it as belonging to the Yupik branch,[http://www.ethnologue.com/show_family.asp?subid=91176 Ethnologue Report for Eskimo–Aleut]{{sfn|Kaplan|1990|p=136}} or as forming a Yupik–Sirenik branch with Yupik.Eváristos Bethlehem. [https://www.academia.edu/101298117/Morphosyntactic_alignment_and_verbal_indexing_in_Inuit_Yupik_Unangan_through_a_diachronic_lens "Morphosyntactic alignment and verbal indexing in Inuit-Yupik-Unangan through a diachronic lens"]. 2023. Many words are formed from entirely different [[Root (linguistics)|root]]s to those in [[Siberian Yupik language|Siberian Yupik]].{{sfn|Menovshchikov|1964|p=42}} In addition, the grammar has several peculiarities compared to the other Eskimoan languages as well as [[Aleut language|Aleut]]. For example, although most Eskaleut languages, including Sirenik's neighboring relative Siberian Yupik,{{sfn|Menovshchikov|1964|p=81}} have [[Dual (grammatical number)|dual number]],{{sfn|Menovshchikov|1964|p=38}} it is not known in Sirenik. The peculiarities amounted to mutual unintelligibility with even its nearest language relatives. This forced Sirenik people to use [[Chukchi language|Chukchi]] as a [[lingua franca]] when speaking with [[Siberian Yupik|neighboring Eskimo peoples]].{{sfn|Menovshchikov|1990|p=70}} Thus, any external contacts for Sirenik people required using a different language: they either resorted to the use of a lingua franca, or used the [[Siberian Yupik language]] (definitely a mutually unintelligible, different language for them, not just a dialect of their own).{{sfn|Menovshchikov|1964|pp=6–7}} This difference from all their language relatives may be the result of a supposed long isolation from other Eskimo groups:{{sfn|Menovshchikov|1962|p=11}}{{sfn|Menovshchikov|1964|p=9}} Sirenik people may have been in contact only with speakers of unrelated languages for many centuries in the past, and their language may have been influenced, especially by non-relative Chukchi.{{sfn|Menovshchikov|1990|p=70}} ==== Internal ==== Although the number of its speakers was very few even at the end of the nineteenth century, the language had at least two [[dialect]]s in the past.{{sfn|Vakhtin|1998|p=162}} === Typological === As for its [[morphological typology]], it has [[Polysynthetic language|polysynthetic]] and [[Incorporation (linguistics)|incorporative]] features, just like the other Eskimoan languages. == Phonology == === Consonants === {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center" ! colspan="2" | ! A description grouped by [[Lexical category|lexical categories]] follows. === Nominal and verbal === Although morphology will be treated grouped into a nominal and a verbal part, many Eskimo languages show features which “crosscut” any such groupings in several aspects: * the [[Ergative–absolutive language|ergative]] structure at verbs is similar to the [[Possession (linguistics)|possessive]] structure at nouns (see section [[#Ergative–absolutive]]); * a physical similarity exists between nominal and verbal personal suffix paradigms, i.e., in most cases, the respective person-number is expressed with the same sequence of phonemes at: ** [[possessive suffix]]es (at nouns) ** verbal suffixes; * nomenverbum-like roots, becoming nominal or verbal only via the suffix they get; * Eskimo texts abound in various kinds of participles (see section [[#Participles]]); ==== Common grammatical categories ==== Some [[Grammatical category|grammatical categories]] (e.g. [[Grammatical person|person]] and [[Grammatical number|number]]) are applicable to both verbal and nominal [[Lexical category|lexical categories]]. Although person and number are expressed in a single suffix, sometimes it can be traced back to consist of a distinct person and a distinct number suffix.{{efn|Person and number in a single suffix, or in two distinct ones.{{sfn|Menovshchikov|1964|p=61}}}} ===== Person ===== [[Inflection|Paradigm]]s can make a distinction in 3rd person for “self”, thus the mere personal suffix (of the verb or noun) can distinguish e.g. ;a nominal example :“He/she takes his/her own dog” versus “He/she takes the dog of another person”. ;a verbal example :“He/she sees himself/herself” versus “He/she sees him/her (another person)” Thus, it can be translated into English (and some other languages) using a [[reflexive pronoun]]. This notion concerns also other concepts in building larger parts of the sentence and the text, see section [[#Usage of third person suffixes]]. ===== Number ===== Although other Eskimo languages know more than the familiar two [[grammatical number]]s, by having also [[Dual (grammatical number)|dual]], Sireniki uses only singular and [[plural]]. Sireniki is, as mentioned above, peculiar in this aspect, alongside [[Greenlandic language|Greenlandic]], within the [[Eskimo–Aleut languages|Eskimo–Aleut language family]],{{sfn|Menovshchikov|1964|p=38}} with even its neighboring [[Siberian Yupik language|Siberian Yupik]] relatives having dual number.{{sfn|Menovshchikov|1964|p=81}} ==== Deictic demonstrative pronouns ==== Sireniki had an unusual wide range of deictic distinctions between up to four distances (near, medial, far and out_of_view) which could be horizontal “una”>”igna”>”ikna”, vertical “mana”>”unygna”>”pikna”, marking a movement like approaching the speaker “ukna”, away from them “agna”, refer to conversational topics be they definite “ugna”>”k’amna”>oov “amna” or indefinite “k’akymna”>”k’agna”>oov “akymna” or describe sth in the past “imna”.{{sfn|Haarmann|2021|p={{page needed|date=July 2024}}}} ==== Building verbs from nouns ==== Suffix -{{IPA|/ɕuɣɨn/}}- meaning “to be similar to sth”: {| class="wikitable" ! Singular 3rd person |- | {{IPA|/juɣ/}} | {{IPA|/juɣɨ t͡ʃ ɨ/}}- | {{IPA|/juɣɨ t͡ʃ ɨtɨn/}} | {{IPA|/juɣɨ t͡ʃ ɨχ/}} |- | man | to be a man | you are a man | he/she is a man |} ===== Verbs built from [[toponym]]s ===== * {{IPA|/imtuk/}} (a [[Toponymy|toponym]]: Imtuk) * {{IPA|/imtux-tɨqɨχ-tɨ-ŋ/}} (I travel to Imtuk.){{efn|Verbs built from [[Toponymy|toponym]]s.{{sfn|Menovshchikov|1964|p=67}}}} === Nominal lexical categories === ==== Grammatical categories ==== Not only the [[Declension|grammatical case]]s of nouns are marked by suffixes, but also the person of possessor (use of possessive pronouns in English) can be expressed by [[agglutination]]. {| class="wikitable" |+ Excerpt from cases and personal possessive form of {{IPA|/taŋaχ/}} (child){{efn|Personal possessive form.{{sfn|Menovshchikov|1964|pp=44–45}}}} | ! [[Ablative case|Ablative]] / [[Instrumental case|Instrumental]] | {{IPA|/taŋamnɨŋ/}} (from my child) | {{IPA|/taŋaχpɨnɨŋ/}} (from your child) |- ! The table illustrates also why Sirenik language is treated as [[Agglutination|agglutinative]] (rather than [[Fusional language|fusional]]). There is no [[grammatical gender]] (or gender-like [[noun class]] system). ===== Case ===== Sireniki is an [[absolutive–ergative language]]. Cases (listed using Menovščikov's numbering): # [[Absolutive case|Absolutive]] # Relative case, playing the role of both [[genitive case]] and [[ergative case]]. # [[Ablative case|Ablative]] / [[Instrumental case|Instrumental]], used also in [[Accusative case|accusative]] structures. # [[Dative case|Dative]] / [[Lative case|Lative]] # [[Locative case|Locative]] # [[Vialis case]], see also [[Prosecutive case]], and [[List of grammatical cases#Motion via|"motion via"]] # [[Equative case|Equative]] (comparative) To see why a single case can play such distinct roles at all, read [[morphosyntactic alignment]], and also [[List of grammatical cases#Morphosyntactic alignment|a short table about it]]. Some finer [[grammatical function]]s are expressed using [[postposition]]s. Most of them are built as a combinations of cases * lative or locative or ablative * combined with relative (used as genitive) in a similar way as we use expressions like "on top of" in English. === Verbal lexical categories === Also at verbs, the morphology is very rich. Suffixes can express [[grammatical mood]]s of the verb (e.g. [[Imperative mood|imperative]], [[Interrogative mood|interrogative]], [[Optative mood|optative]]), and also negation, [[Grammatical tense|tense]], [[Grammatical aspect|aspect]], the [[Grammatical person|person]] of subject and object. Some examples (far from being comprehensive): {| class="wikitable" ! rowspan=3 | Phonology ! rowspan=3 | Meaning ! colspan=4 | Grammatical notes |- ! colspan=2 | Person, number of ! rowspan=2 | [[Grammatical mood|Mood]] ! rowspan=2 | Others |- ! subject ! object |- | {{IPA|/aʁaʁɨ-tɨqɨχ-tɨ-mkɨn/}} | I lead you | Singular 1st person | Singular 2nd person | Indicative | |- | {{IPA|/aʁaʁɨ-ɕuk-ɨ-mɕi/}} | Let me lead you | Singular 1st person | Singular 2nd person | Imperative{{efn|Imperative.{{sfn|Menovshchikov|1964|p=86}}}} | |- | {{IPA|/nɨŋɨ-sɨɣɨŋ-sɨn/}} | Don't you see me? | Singular 2nd person | Singular 1st person | [[Interrogative]] | Negative polarity{{efn|name=neg|Negation form of a verb.{{sfn|Menovshchikov|1964|p=89}}}} |} The rich set of [[morpheme]]s makes it possible to build huge verbs whose meaning could be expressed (in most of widely known languages) as whole sentences (consisting of more words) . Sireniki – like the other Eskimo languages – has [[Polysynthetic language|polysynthetic]] and [[Incorporation (linguistics)|incorporative]] features, in many forms, among others [[polypersonal agreement]]. ==== Grammatical categories ==== The [[Polysynthetic language|polysynthetic]] and [[Incorporation (linguistics)|incorporative]] features mentioned above manifest themselves in most of the ways Sirenik language can express [[Grammatical category|grammatical categories]]. ===== Transitivity ===== For background, see [[Transitivity (grammatical category)|transitivity]]. (Remember also section [[#Ergative–absolutive]].) See also Nicole Tersis and Shirley Carter-Thomas (2005).{{sfn|Tersis|Carter-Thomas|2005}} ===== Polarity ===== Even the [[grammatical polarity]] can be expressed by adding a suffix to the verb. An example for negative polarity: the negation form of the verb {{IPA|/aʁaʁ-/}} (to go): * {{IPA|/juɣ aʁaχ-tɨqɨχ-tɨ-χ/}} (the man walks) * {{IPA|/juɣ aʁaʁ-ɨ-tɨ-χ/}} (the man does not walk){{efn|name=neg}} ===== Aspect ===== [[Grammatical aspect]]: * {{IPA|/aftalʁa-'''qɨstaχ'''-/}} (to work '''slowly''') and {{IPA|/aftalʁa-'''qɨstaχ'''-tɨqɨχ-tɨ-χ/}} (he works '''slowly'''),{{efn|Suffix -{{IPA|/qɨstaχ-/}} for slow action [[Grammatical aspect|aspect]].{{sfn|Menovshchikov|1964|p=72}}}} from {{IPA|/aftalʁa-/}} (to work) ===== Modality ===== Also [[linguistic modality]] can be expressed by suffixes. [[Modal verb]]s like "want to", "wish to" etc. do not even exist:{{efn|name=mod|Modality.{{sfn|Menovshchikov|1964|p=68}}}} {| class="wikitable" |+Suffix -jux- (to want to): | {{IPA|/aftalʁaχ-/}} (to work) | {{IPA|/aftalʁaʁ-'''jux'''-/}} (to '''want''' to work){{efn|name=mod}} |- | {{IPA|/aftalʁaχ-tɨqɨχ-tɨ-ŋ/}} (I work){{efn|Present tense.{{sfn|Menovshchikov|1964|p=61}}}} | {{IPA|/aftalʁaʁ-'''jux'''-tɨqɨχ-tɨ-ŋ/}} (I '''want''' to work){{efn|name=mod}} |} The table illustrates also why Sirenik is treated as [[Agglutination|agglutinative]] (rather than [[Fusional language|fusional]]). ===== Voice ===== Four [[grammatical voice]]s are mentioned in:{{efn|name=voice|[[Grammatical voice]]s.{{sfn|Menovshchikov|1964|pp=78–80}}}} ;active ;passive :confer {{IPA|-/ɕi/-}} that variant of [[Siberian Yupik]] which is spoken by Ungazigmit{{sfn|Rubtsova|1954|pp=121–123}} ;middle (medial) ;causative :{{IPA|/malikam aʁaχ-'''ɕaχ'''-tɨqɨχ-tɨ-ʁa kɨtuɣi qurŋi-nu/}} (Malika '''make'''s Kitugi go to the reindeer.){{efn|name=voice}} all of them are expressed by agglutination, thus, no separate words are required. === Participles === A distinction between two kinds of [[participle]]s ([[adverbial participle]] and [[adjectival participle]]) makes sense in Sireniki (just like in [[Hungarian grammar|Hungarian]], see [[:hu:Határozói igenév|határozói igenév]] and [[:hu:Melléknévi igenév|melléknévi igenév]] for detailed description of these concepts; or in [[Russian grammar|Russian]], see [[:ru:Деепричастие|деепричастие]] and [[:ru:Причастие (часть речи)|причастие]]). Sireniki has many kinds of participles in both categories. In the following, they will be listed, grouped by the relation between the “dependent action” and “main action” (or by other meanings beyond this, e.g. [[Linguistic modality|modality]]) – following the terminology of Menovschikov (1964).{{sfn|Menovshchikov|1964}} A sentence with a participle can be imagined as simulating a subordinating [[compound sentence (linguistics)|compound sentence]] where the action described in the [[dependent clause]] relates somehow to the action described in the [[Independent clause|main clause]]. In English, an [[adverbial clause]] may express [[Adverbial clause#Kinds of adverbial clauses|reason, purpose, condition, succession etc.]], and a [[relative clause]] can express many meanings, too. In an analogous way, in Sireniki Eskimo language, the "dependent action" (expressed by the adverbial participle in the sentence element called [[adverbial]], or expressed by the adjectival participle in the sentence element called attribute) relates somehow to the “main action” (expressed by the verb in the sentence element called [[Predicate (grammar)|predicate]]), and the participles will be listed below grouped by this relation (or by other meanings beyond this, e.g. [[Linguistic modality|modality]]). ==== Adverbial participles ==== They can be translated into English e.g. by using an appropriate [[adverbial clause]]. There are many of them, with various meanings. An interesting feature: they can have person and number. The person of the dependent action need not coincide with that of the main action. An example (meant in the British English usage of “shall / should” in the 1st person: here, conveying only conditional, but no necessity or morality): {| class="wikitable" |+ “I” versus “we” | {{IPA|/mɨŋa iŋɨjaxtɨk-t͡ʃɨ-ʁɨjɨqɨɣɨ-ma, ajvɨʁaʁjuʁuχtɨki/}} |- | If ''I'' were a marksman, ''we'' should kill walrus |} Another example (with a different adverbial participle): {| class="wikitable" |+ “he/she” versus “they” | {{IPA|/ɨ̆ l̥tɨʁinɨq ȷ̊an, upʃuχtɨqɨχtɨʁij/}} |- | when ''he/she'' sings, ''they'' keep frightening him/her |} They will be discussed in more details below. ===== Reason, purpose or circumstance of action ===== An adverbial participle “explaining reason, purpose or circumstance of action” is expressed by suffix -{{IPA|/lɨ/}}- / -{{IPA|/ l̥ɨ/}}- (followed by appropriate person-number suffix). Examples:{{efn|Adverbial participle -{{IPA|/lɨ/}}- / - {{IPA|/l̥ɨ/}}- “explaining reason, purpose or circumstance of action”.{{sfn|Menovshchikov|1964|pp=90–91}}}} {| class="wikitable" ! rowspan=2 | Persons ! colspan=2 | Sentence |- ! Adverbial participle ! Adverbial participle ! Verb |- | {{IPA|/nɨŋitu l̥ɨku}} | {{IPA|pɨjɨkɨŋa/}} |- | To examine him/her2 (another being) | he/she1 went |} ===== Dependent action ends just before main action begins ===== Using the adverbial participle -{{IPA|/ja/}}- / -{{IPA|/ɕa/}}-, the dependent action (expressed by the adverbial participle in the [[sentence element]] called [[adverbial]]) finishes just before the main action (expressed by the verb in the sentence element called [[Predicate (grammar)|predicate]]) begins.{{efn|name=endjustbeg|Adverbial participle -{{IPA|/ja/}}- / -{{IPA|/ɕa/}}- (dependent action ends just before main action begins).{{sfn|Menovshchikov|1964|pp=91–92}}}} ===== Dependent action begins before main action, but they continue together till end ===== It can be expressed by suffix -{{IPA|/inɨq ȷ̊a/}}-.{{efn|name=endjustbeg}} Examples: {| class="wikitable" | {{IPA|/nukɨ l̥piɣt͡ʃɨʁaʁɨm aninɨq ȷ̊ami qamt͡ʃɨni tiɣɨmɨra(x)/}} |- | the boy, going out [of the house], took his [own] sledge [with himself]) |} where {| class="wikitable" |+ {{IPA|/nukɨ l̥piɣt͡ʃɨʁaʁɨm/}} ! Phonology ! Syntax ! Semantics |- | {{IPA|/tɨɣɨˈraχ/}} | verb | he/she took something |- | -{{IPA|/mɨ/}}- / -{{IPA|/ɨmɨ/}}- | tense suffix | past tense (not the “near past” one) |} Another example: {| class="wikitable" | {{IPA|/ɨ̆ l̥tɨʁinɨq ȷ̊an, upʃuχtɨqɨχtɨʁij/}} |- | when he/she sings, they keep frightening him/her |} ===== Conditional ===== Dependent action is conditional: it does not takes place, although it would (either really, or provided that some—maybe irreal—conditions would hold). Confer also [[conditional sentence]]. Sireniki Eskimo has several adverbial participles to express that.{{efn|Adverbial participles conveying conditional dependent action.{{sfn|Menovshchikov|1964|pp=92–93}}}} We can distinguish them according to the concerned condition (conveyed by the dependent action): it may be * either real (possible to take place in the future) * or irreal (it would take place only if some other irreal condition would hold) ====== Real ====== It is expressed with suffix -{{IPA|/qɨɣɨ/}}- / -{{IPA|/kɨɣɨ/}}-, let us see e.g. a paradigm beginning with {{IPA|/aʁa-qɨɣɨ-ma/}} (if I get off / depart); {{IPA|/aʁa-qɨɣɨ-pi/}} (if you get off / depart): {| class="wikitable" ! rowspan=2 colspan=2 | ! colspan=2 | Number |- ! Singular ! Plural |- ! rowspan=3 | Person ! 1st | {{IPA|/aʁa-qɨɣɨ-ma/}} | {{IPA|/aʁa-qɨɣɨ-mta/}} |- ! 2nd | {{IPA|/aʁa-qɨɣɨ-pi/}} | {{IPA|/aʁa-qɨɣɨ-pɨɕi/}} |- ! 3rd | {{IPA|/aʁa-qɨɣɨ-mi/}} | {{IPA|/aʁa-qɨɣɨ-mɨŋ/}} |} ====== Irrealis ====== Compare with [[counterfactual conditional]]. Sireniki can compress it into an adverbial participle: it is expressed with suffix -{{IPA|/ɣɨjɨqɨɣɨ/}}- / -{{IPA|/majɨqɨɣɨ/}}-. The dependent action is expressed with an adverbial participle. The main action is conveyed by the verb. If also the main action is conditional (a typical usage), than it can be expressed with a verb of conditional mood. The persons need not coincide. An example (meant in the British English usage of “shall / should” in the 1st person: here, conveying only conditional, but no necessity or morality): {| class="wikitable" | {{IPA|/mɨŋa iŋɨjaxtɨk-t͡ʃɨ-ʁɨjɨqɨɣɨ-ma, ajvɨʁaʁjuʁuχtɨki/}} |- | If I were a marksman, we should kill walrus. |} The example in details: Dependent action: {| class="wikitable" |+ {{IPA|/iŋɨjaxtɨk-t͡ʃɨ-ʁɨjɨqɨɣɨ-ma/}} (if I were a marksman) ! Phonology ! Syntax ! Semantics |- | {{IPA|/iŋˈɨːjaxta/}} | noun | marksman |- | -{{IPA|/t͡ʃɨ/}}- | suffix [[#Building verbs from nouns|building a verb out of a noun]] | [[#Predicative form of a noun|predicative form]] of noun |- | -{{IPA|/ɣɨjɨqɨɣɨ/}}- / -{{IPA|/majɨqɨɣɨ/}}- | the suffix of the adverbial participle | irreal condition |- | -{{IPA|/ma/}} | person-number suffix for adverbial participles in the intransitive conjugation | subject 1st person |} ==== Adjectival participles ==== There are several kinds of adjectival participles. * {{IPA|/imtuɡnu aʁaqt͡ʃɨχ qɨmɨ l̥ɨʁaχ utɨχt͡ʃɨmɨt͡ʃɨχ/}}: "The sledge [that went to Imtuk] returned." * {{IPA|/juɣ qavɨ l̥ɨʁɨχ nɨŋɨsɨmɨrɨqa/}}: "I saw [perceived] a sleeping man." They can be used not only attributively, as in the above examples, but also predicatively:{efn|Attribute versus predicative usage of adjectival participles.{{sfn|Menovshchikov|1964|p=95}} * {{IPA|/juɣ qavɨ l̥ɨʁɨχ/}}: The man is sleeping. ===== Modality ===== The djectival participle -{{IPA|/kajux/}} / -{{IPA|/qajux/}} conveys a meaning "able to", related rather to [[Linguistic modality|modality]] than to the relation of dependent action and main action).{{efn|Adjectival participle -{{IPA|/kajux/}} / -{{IPA|/qajux/}} (able to).{{sfn|Menovshchikov|1964|p=97}}}} * {{IPA|/taŋaʁaχ pijɨ'''kajux''' pijɨxtɨqɨχtɨχ l̥mɨnɨŋ/}}: "A child who is able to walk moves around spontaneously." == Syntax == Like many Eskimoan languages, Sireniki is an [[ergative–absolutive language]].
